title: Reproducible Python Environments
intro: 'It worked in my notebook' is the ML version of 'works on my machine'. Pinning the exact environment a model was trained in is the first step to being able to reproduce — or even load — it later.

steps.prompt: Create an isolated virtual environment called venv for this project.
steps.explanation: A self-contained Python installation, separate from the system Python and other projects.
steps.why: Installing packages globally means every project shares (and fights over) one set of versions. One venv per project keeps upgrades in one from silently breaking another.

steps.explanation: Your prompt shows (venv); 'python' and 'pip' now refer to the environment's copies.
steps.why: Forgetting to activate is the most common reason 'I installed it but it says module not found' — pip installed into a different Python than the one running your script.

steps.fake_output:
Collecting scikit-learn==1.5.1
Collecting pandas==2.2.2
...
Successfully installed pandas-2.2.2 scikit-learn-1.5.1 ...
steps.explanation: Exact versions from requirements.txt are installed.
steps.why: Pickled scikit-learn models often won't load — or worse, silently behave differently — under a different library version than they were trained with. Exact pins (==) matter far more for ML than for typical web apps.

steps.prompt: After adding a package, record the exact versions of everything installed.
steps.explanation: Every installed package, including transitive dependencies, pinned with ==.
steps.why: pip freeze captures everything, which is great for reproducibility but noisy. Tools like pip-tools (requirements.in → requirements.txt) or poetry.lock separate 'what I asked for' from 'exactly what got resolved'.

steps.prompt: For a project using Poetry instead, resolve and lock dependencies after editing pyproject.toml.
steps.explanation: poetry.lock records the exact resolved versions and hashes.
steps.why: Commit the lock file. Training and serving environments built from the same lock file are one of the simplest defenses against training/serving skew caused by library differences.

steps.prompt: A data-science teammate uses conda (common for CUDA/scientific stacks). Export their exact environment to share it.
steps.explanation: Includes conda and pip packages, and non-Python dependencies like the CUDA toolkit.
steps.why: conda manages non-Python libraries (CUDA, MKL) that pip can't — a big reason it's popular for GPU work. Add --no-builds for an export that's more portable across operating systems.
